title: Tetanus: wound prophylaxis and established disease
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Wounds: give Td if fewer than 3 prior doses, unknown history, or last dose 10 years ago (5 years for dirty wounds); add TIG 250 IU for dirty wounds in the incompletely vaccinated or immunodeficient. Established tetanus: human TIG, wound debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines and magnesium for spasms, early airway control, then complete vaccination.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Clinical diagnosis; there is no confirmatory test. Trismus (lockjaw) or risus sardonicus, or painful muscle spasms, usually with a history of a wound, which may have been trivial or forgotten.
Incubation usually 3 to 21 days (median 7). Short incubation and rapid progression from first symptom to spasms predict severe disease.
Generalised spasms and opisthotonus are triggered by touch, noise and light; consciousness is preserved. Laryngeal spasm can cause sudden airway obstruction.
Autonomic dysfunction in severe cases: labile hypertension and tachycardia alternating with bradycardia and hypotension, sweating, fever.
Neonatal tetanus (first 28 days): inability to suck, stiffness and spasms after unclean delivery or cord care.

sections.title: Wound prophylaxis
items: Clean, minor wounds: give a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine if vaccination history is unknown or fewer than 3 doses, or if 10 years or more since the last dose. TIG is never needed.

All other wounds (dirt, soil, faeces or saliva contamination including animal or human bites, puncture or penetrating wounds, burns, crush injuries, compound fractures, devitalised tissue): vaccine if history unknown or fewer than 3 doses, or 5 years or more since the last dose.
Add human TIG 250 IU IM for these dirty or major wounds if history is unknown or fewer than 3 doses, or the patient has HIV or severe immunodeficiency (regardless of vaccination history).
Vaccine: Td 0.5 mL IM (Td has replaced TT in India) from 7 years of age; DPT (or DTaP) under 7 years. Give TIG and vaccine with separate syringes at separate sites.
Clean and debride the wound. Antibiotics do not prevent tetanus. Arrange the remaining primary doses for anyone incompletely vaccinated.

sections.title: Established tetanus: first hours
items: Assess the airway immediately; laryngeal spasm and aspiration are the early killers. Admit to ICU or HDU; if spasms threaten ventilation, intubate and ventilate. Early tracheostomy is preferred for prolonged ventilation because the endotracheal tube itself provokes spasm.
Nurse in a quiet, dim room with minimal handling; group procedures together under sedation.
Give human TIG as soon as possible, before wound debridement.
Start benzodiazepines titrated to spasm control, and metronidazole.
Clean and debride the wound (after TIG); remove foreign bodies and necrotic tissue.

sections.title: Antitoxin, antibiotics and vaccination
items: Human TIG 500 IU IM (or IV, depending on the preparation) as soon as possible (WHO). Higher doses of 3000 to 6000 IU IM are also widely used.
Metronidazole (preferred): 500 mg IV or orally 6-hourly for 7 to 10 days; children 7.5 mg/kg per dose 6-hourly (maximum 500 mg per dose).
Alternative: penicillin G 100,000 to 200,000 IU/kg/day IV in 2 to 4 divided doses. Tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin, cephalosporins and chloramphenicol are also effective.

Tetanus does not induce immunity: give age-appropriate tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine 0.5 mL IM at a different site from TIG, then second and third doses 1 to 2 months and 6 to 12 months later if never fully vaccinated.

sections.title: Spasm, autonomic instability and airway
items: Benzodiazepines first line: adults diazepam 5 mg IV or lorazepam 2 mg IV increments, titrated to spasm control without excessive sedation; children 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg every 2 to 6 hours, titrated upward. Very large doses (up to 600 mg/day of diazepam) may be needed, which requires ventilatory support.
Magnesium sulphate, alone or with benzodiazepines, for spasm and autonomic dysfunction: 5 g (or 75 mg/kg) IV loading, then 2 to 3 g per hour until spasms are controlled.
On magnesium, check the patellar reflex regularly; loss of the reflex marks the top of the therapeutic range (about 4 mmol/L), so reduce the dose. Watch for respiratory depression.
Autonomic dysfunction: magnesium or morphine. Avoid propranolol (hypotension, sudden death); esmolol is the only beta-blocker recommended.
Refractory spasms: sedation with neuromuscular blockade and mechanical ventilation. Other agents include baclofen, dantrolene and short-acting barbiturates.

sections.title: Monitoring and supportive care
items: Continuous ECG, BP (arterial line if autonomic storm), SpO2 and respiratory rate; spasm frequency and sedation score.
Fluids and early enteral nutrition: spasms create high metabolic demands and a catabolic state.
Prevent complications: aspiration pneumonia, ventilator-associated infection, pressure sores, venous thromboembolism, rhabdomyolysis and renal injury.
Spasms typically continue for 1 to 2 weeks and recovery takes weeks; survival improves greatly if the patient is supported through this period.

sections.title: Prevention
items: WHO recommends 6 doses for lifelong protection: 3 primary doses in infancy plus boosters at 12 to 23 months, 4 to 7 years and 9 to 15 years.
India UIP: DPT at 6, 10 and 14 weeks (as pentavalent), DPT boosters at 16 to 24 months and 5 to 6 years, and Td at 10 and 16 years.
Pregnancy: 2 doses of Td 4 weeks apart, or 1 booster if vaccinated with 2 doses in the previous 3 years; clean delivery and cord care prevent neonatal tetanus.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving TIG for clean minor wounds, or omitting it for dirty wounds in the unvaccinated.
Giving antibiotics instead of vaccine and TIG to prevent tetanus.
Debriding the wound before giving TIG.
Discharging a tetanus survivor without starting vaccination.
Heavy sedation without the ability to ventilate.

drugs.name: Td vaccine (tetanus and diphtheria toxoid)
drugs.notes: Age 7 years and over; DPT or DTaP under 7 years. Separate site from TIG.

drugs.name: Human tetanus immunoglobulin (prophylaxis)
drugs.notes: Dirty or major wounds with unknown or fewer than 3 prior doses, HIV or severe immunodeficiency.

drugs.name: Human tetanus immunoglobulin (treatment)
drugs.dose: 500 IU IM or IV (per preparation), single dose, as early as possible
drugs.notes: WHO dose; 3000 to 6000 IU IM is also used. Give before wound debridement.

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.dose: 500 mg IV or orally 6-hourly for 7 to 10 days; children 7.5 mg/kg 6-hourly (maximum 500 mg per dose)

drugs.name: Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G)
drugs.dose: 100,000 to 200,000 IU/kg/day IV in 2 to 4 divided doses

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: Adults 5 mg IV increments titrated to effect; children 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg every 2 to 6 hours
drugs.notes: Up to 600 mg/day may be needed; ensure airway and ventilation.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: Adults 2 mg IV increments titrated to spasm control

drugs.name: Magnesium sulphate
drugs.dose: 5 g (or 75 mg/kg) IV loading dose, then 2 to 3 g per hour
drugs.notes: Monitor patellar reflex; reduce if areflexic (about 4 mmol/L). Watch respiration.
